questions.title: What is the precise legal distinction between the 'right-to-control' theory rejected in Ciminelli and the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory accepted here?
questions.question_body: I am struggling to understand why the court distinguishes these two theories so sharply. Both seem to involve lying to get someone to make a financial decision. In *Ciminelli*, the Supreme Court said depriving someone of 'valuable economic information' isn't enough for fraud because it's not a 'traditional property interest.' However, in this case (*Constantinescu*), the court says the indictment alleges defendants lied to induce followers to buy stocks, which constitutes obtaining 'money or property.' If the core mechanism in both cases is deception regarding economic data leading to a transaction, why does one fail as a 'property interest' claim while the other succeeds? Is the key difference simply that *Kousisis* involves an actual transfer of funds (buying stock), whereas *Ciminelli* involved bidding on government contracts where no money changed hands immediately?

questions.title: Does the lack of net pecuniary loss for the victim invalidate an intent-to-defraud charge under Kousisis?
questions.question_body: The defendants argued that they couldn't be guilty because they didn't intend to 'harm' their victims financially—they just wanted to profit themselves. The court cites *Kousisis* stating that fraud doesn't require a victim to suffer an economic loss or for the defendant to seek a net loss for the victim. This confuses me: if I lie and sell you a stock at fair market value (so you don't lose money relative to what you paid), but I made money by dumping my shares earlier, how is there an 'injury'? Does *Kousisis* effectively mean that any intentional deception resulting in a transfer of money satisfies the 'harm' element, even if the victim received equivalent value in return? How does this align with traditional common-law notions of fraud requiring damage?

questions.title: How does 18 U.S.C. § 1348 incorporate mail/wire fraud precedents like Ciminelli and Kousisis given statutory text differences?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that § 1348 (securities fraud) 'borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes' (§§ 1341/1343). However, I know that securities fraud has its own specific elements regarding connection with securities transactions. Why did the Fifth Circuit feel compelled to rely so heavily on general wire/mail fraud cases like *Ciminelli* and *Kousisis* rather than interpreting § 1348 independently? Are there specific textual hooks in § 1348 that mandate this borrowing, or is this purely judicial interpretation based on historical legislative intent? Could Congress have written § 1348 differently to avoid these interpretations?

questions.title: Is 'deprivation of potentially valuable economic information' ever actionable under federal fraud statutes post-Ciminelli?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed the indictment partly because it felt defendants only deprived followers of information. The appellate court reversed, saying this case wasn't about information deprivation but about obtaining money via fraudulent inducement. My confusion lies in the boundary: At what point does a scheme shift from being merely about withholding/misleading on information (which seems barred by *Ciminelli*) to being about obtaining property? If I tell someone false info about a stock's potential so they buy it, aren't I still primarily depriving them of accurate information? What specific factual allegation transforms this from an informational wrong into a property theft under current precedent?

questions.title: What is the scope of review for sufficiency of an indictment versus sufficiency of evidence at trial?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions reviewing sufficiency de novo and taking allegations as true. As a student trying to distinguish procedural stages, I want to confirm: Does this reversal mean the government has now proven its case beyond a reasonable doubt? Or does it simply mean they met a very low threshold at this stage (alleging facts plausibly)? If we assume all allegations are true per this standard, why was there ever doubt about whether they alleged a crime? Specifically, how does this standard protect defendants compared to what would happen if we looked at actual evidence later?

questions.title: Can a defendant be convicted of securities fraud if they provided something of equal value in exchange for the victim's money?
questions.question_body: *Kousisis* suggests that providing something of equal value doesn't negate fraud if there was deception. In this pump-and-dump scenario, defendants sold real shares (even if manipulated) rather than nothingness. If an investor buys $100 worth of stock for $100, but bought it based on lies about trading volume or insider knowledge, is that legally indistinguishable from stealing $100 cash? How does criminal law treat 'fair exchange achieved through lies' versus 'theft by force,' especially when no net wealth transfer occurred for the buyer?
